a: he keeps his anger ready for his enemies
t: Keeps anger, or removes enemies?
p: The Hebrew says the LORD keeps anger for his enemies; the Greek says he removes them.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the words "and he keeps" are legible; the rest of the line is restored)
readings.en: and he keeps it for his enemies
readings.plain: he keeps his anger ready for his enemies

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:2)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξαίρων αὐτὸς τοὺς ἐχθροὺς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and he himself takes away his enemies
readings.plain: he himself takes his enemies away

why: The Hebrew participle is clear and has a known use (Leviticus 19:18; Psalm 103:9). The Greek verb means "lift out, remove" and looks like a translator's smoothing of a verb he found strange for God.
b: In Mur88 only the letters "and he keeps it" (wnwtr hw') are fully readable; "for his enemies" is a restoration, so the scroll cannot be cited for that phrase. 4QXIIg does not preserve the verse.

a: He goes his way in gale and storm
t: Gale and storm, or "completion" and "shaking"?
p: The Hebrew has "in gale and in storm." The Greek has "in completion and in shaking."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("and in the storm" legible; "in the gale" restored)
readings.en: in whirlwind and in storm is his way
readings.plain: He goes his way in gale and storm

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:3)
readings.orig: ἐν συντελείᾳ καὶ ἐν συνσεισμῷ ἡ ὁδὸς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: in completion and in shaking is his way
readings.plain: His way is in an ending and a shaking

why: The Greek words mean "end, completion" and "shaking, earthquake." The translator may have read the same consonants differently or paraphrased; the cause is not clear. The Masoretic reading fits the storm picture of the next lines (cloud as the dust of his feet) and is what the scroll shows where it is readable.

t: "Great of power": two spellings
p: The Hebrew data record a second spelling of "and great"; the meaning is the same.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the same spelling, legible)
readings.en: and great of power
readings.plain: his power is great

readings.w: The second spelling listed in the Ketiv/Qere notes of the Hebrew data this site draws on (STEPBible, in texts/auto)
readings.en: and great of power
readings.plain: his power is great

why: The two forms differ only in how the word for "great" is spelled and vowelled. The Plain English Translation is the same either way.

a: He scolds the sea, and it goes dry.
t: Scolds the sea, or threatens it?
p: The Hebrew says he scolds the sea and dries it. The Greek says he threatens it and dries it, and varies the repeated "withers."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("rebuking in the sea" and "and he dried it" legible)
readings.en: rebuking the sea, and he made it dry
readings.plain: He scolds the sea, and it goes dry.

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:4)
readings.en: threatening the sea and drying it
readings.plain: He threatens the sea and dries it.

why: The Greek apeilon ("threatening") is a milder word for ga'ar than the Hebrew's "rebuke," and the Greek uses two different verbs for the one Hebrew 'umlal, which the Plain English Translation keeps as one word twice. The Hebrew is clear and the scroll agrees with it where legible.
b: The Greek of the next lines also differs: it has "was made few" (oligothe) and "failed" (exelipen) for the one Hebrew verb 'umlal ("withers") that the Plain English Translation keeps twice, and "the blossoming things of Lebanon" for "the flower of Lebanon." In Mur88 "he dried it," "all the rivers," and both "withers" are legible; "he dried up," Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon are restored.

a: The earth is lifted up in front of him
t: Lifted up, or drawn back?
p: The Hebrew says the earth is lifted up. The Greek says the earth drew back.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("and is lifted up" and "from his face" legible; "the earth" restored)
readings.en: and the earth is lifted up from his face
readings.plain: The earth is lifted up in front of him

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:5)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀνεστάλη ἡ γῆ ἀπὸ προσώπου αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and the earth drew back from his face
readings.plain: The earth drew back from him

why: The Hebrew verb nasa' ("lift") can also mean "heave" or "bear"; the Greek verb means "draw back, shrink." The Greek is a fair sense of a shaken earth, and the Masoretic verb is the harder and older reading, shown by the scroll.

t: A stronghold, or "to those who wait for him"?
p: The Hebrew says the LORD is a stronghold to those who shelter in him. The Greek has no stronghold and says "good to those who wait for him."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("good," "for a stronghold," "in the day of trouble" and "those who take refuge" legible); 4Q82 ("in the day of trouble" legible; "those who take refuge" spelled with a waw)
readings.en: good is the LORD, for a stronghold in the day of trouble
readings.plain: he is a stronghold

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:7)
readings.orig: χρηστὸς Κύριος τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν αὐτὸν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ θλίψεως, καὶ γινώσκων τοὺς εὐλαβουμένους αὐτόν
readings.en: good is the LORD to those who wait for him in the day of trouble, and knowing those who revere him
readings.plain: he is good to those who wait for him in the day of trouble, and he knows those who revere him

why: The Greek has nothing for ma'oz ("stronghold"); it makes the line say whom the LORD is good to, and it gives "take refuge" the sense "revere." The word ma'oz matters to the book, since it returns in 3:11, so the fuller Hebrew line is followed. Both scrolls agree with it where their letters are readable.
b: The Hebrew continues "and knowing those who take refuge in him"; the Greek gives "knowing those who revere him."

a: he will make a full end of her place
t: Her place, or those who rise up?
p: The Hebrew has "her place" (feminine). The Greek has "those who rise up" and no "her."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the letters are fully legible)
readings.en: he will make a complete end of her place
readings.plain: he will make a full end of her place

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:8)
readings.en: he will make an end, of those who rise up
readings.plain: he will make a full end of those who rise up against him

why: Mur88 reads the same consonants (mqwmh) as the Masoretic Text, so "her place" is the older Hebrew. The Greek probably read the same letters differently, as qamim, "those who rise," and dropped the feminine ending, a smoother thing to say about enemies.
b: Whether "her place" means Nineveh's place, the place of the plotters, or something else is open (see the note on this verse).

t: Will trouble rise twice, or will he avenge twice?
p: The Hebrew says trouble will not rise a second time. The Greek says he will not take vengeance twice.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 and 4Q82 (the letters lo' taqum are fully legible in both)
readings.en: affliction will not rise a second time
readings.plain: Trouble will not arise twice

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:9)
readings.orig: οὐκ ἐκδικήσει δὶς ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἐν θλίψει
readings.en: he will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in affliction
readings.plain: He will not take vengeance twice for the same thing

why: Two scrolls from the Judean Desert (Mur88 and 4QXIIg) have the Masoretic consonants. The Greek translator took the verb as a form of naqam ("avenge"), a word that the poem has used three times in verse 2, or paraphrased the idea that God's judgment is complete and not repeated.
b: Readers have taken the Hebrew line three ways: (1) Assyria's final fall is so complete that trouble from it will not come a second time to Judah; (2) the LORD's judgment on Nineveh will not need repeating; (3) Judah's affliction by Assyria will not occur again (some read it against Sennacherib's army, destroyed outside Jerusalem, 2 Kings 19:35). The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew and does not choose.

a: and soaked like drunkards in their drink
t: Drunkards, or no drunkards?
p: The Hebrew has "soaked like drunkards in their drink." The Greek leaves the phrase out and reads the verse differently.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (sbw'ym 'klw legible)
readings.en: and as their drink they are drunk
readings.plain: and soaked like drunkards in their drink

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:10)
readings.orig: ὅτι ἕως θεμελίου αὐτοῦ χερσωθήσεται, καὶ ὡς σμῖλαξ περιπλεκομένη βρωθήσεται
readings.en: for down to its foundation it will be laid waste, and like entwined bindweed it will be eaten up
readings.plain: It will be laid waste down to its foundation and eaten up like a tangled vine

why: The Hebrew is hard (the word sove' "drink" and sevu'im "drunk" are the same root twice) and the Greek seems to have given up on it, reading the first part as "down to its foundation" and making "thorns" into a creeping weed (smilax). Mur88 has the Masoretic consonants, which supports that the Hebrew reading is old, however hard.
b: The Hebrew line is one of the hardest in the book. Commentators reread or emend it in several ways; the Plain English Translation takes it as "even while they are tangled and drunk" and does not rewrite the Hebrew. Nahum 3:11 also uses drunkenness as a picture of a doomed city.

t: A worthless adviser, or "plotting hostile evils"?
p: The Hebrew has "an adviser of worthlessness." The Greek has "plotting hostile evils" and no such title.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("counseled" and "beliyya'al" legible)
readings.en: a counselor of worthlessness
readings.plain: a worthless adviser

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:11)
readings.en: plotting hostile evils
readings.plain: plotting hostile evils

why: The Greek turns the plotter into "a plan" and gives no equivalent of beliyya'al. In 1:15 the Greek renders the same word as "to wearing out, to decay" (eis palaiosin), apparently from a root meaning "wear out." The Masoretic line keeps the word that links 1:11 and 1:15, which the Plain English Translation follows.
b: The Greek of the whole line is "from you will go out a plan against the LORD, plotting hostile evils." In Mur88 "from you," "went out," "against," "counseled" and "beliyya'al" are legible; "plotted," "the LORD" and "evil" are restored.

a: I have brought you low, but I will not bring you low again
t: "I have brought you low," or "your report will not be heard"?
p: The Hebrew says the LORD has brought "you" low and will not do so again. The Greek has something else, about a report.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (the second half of the verse; Mur88 has the words "I will not" and "again" in readable letters but the verb itself is a restoration)
readings.en: and I have afflicted you, I will not afflict you again
readings.plain: I have brought you low, but I will not bring you low again

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:12)
readings.orig: καὶ ἡ ἀκοή σου οὐκ ἐνακουσθήσεται ἔτι
readings.en: and your report will no longer be heard
readings.plain: and news of you will not be heard again

why: The Greek has also "ruling over many waters" for "sound and many." The Greek reflects either a different Hebrew word or a free rendering, and it fits Nineveh as the person addressed. The Masoretic reading fits a promise to Judah. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: Because the Greek makes "you" Nineveh and the Hebrew most naturally makes "you" Judah, this variant decides the debate on the addressee for those who follow the Greek.

t: "You are of no weight," or "swift"?
p: The Hebrew says the city counts for nothing. The Greek has a word "swift" that it joins to the next verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (Mur88 has this word only as a restoration)
readings.en: for you are light, you are worth nothing
readings.plain: for you count for nothing

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:14, ending)
readings.en: because swift [ones]
readings.plain: because swift

why: The Hebrew qallota comes from qalal, "be light, be of little weight," which fits the grave and the cut-off name. The Greek ends verse 14 with "because swift" and begins verse 15 with "Look, on the mountains," so it joins "swift" to "the feet" of the herald. Both are plausible readings of the same letters; the Hebrew reading makes better sense of the end of the verse.
b: Hebrew qalot ("swift ones") and qallota ("you are light") differ little. If the Greek is right, the herald's feet are swift (as in 2 Samuel 2:18, where Asahel was "swift of foot") and the line belongs to 1:15.

t: "He is cut off" or "It is finished"?
p: The Hebrew says the worthless one is cut off completely. The Greek reads the same letters as a verb and moves them to the next chapter.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (Mur88 has the words only as a restoration)
readings.en: all of him is cut off
readings.plain: He is cut off completely

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:1; the Greek chapter 2 begins with these words)
readings.en: it is finished, it is taken away
readings.plain: It is finished. It is taken away.

why: The Hebrew consonants klh can be read kullo ("all of him") or kalah ("it is finished"). The Masoretic pointing makes it the former, and a person (the "worthless one") is the subject of the whole verse. The Greek read the second and started a new verse with it. The Greek carries only these last words into its chapter 2 (Greek 2:1); the rest of English 1:15 stays in Greek chapter 1. The Hebrew Bible's own chapter 2 begins earlier, at "Look! On the mountains" (see the numbering note).

a: will never again pass through you
t: "To pass": two spellings, and the Greek ending
p: The Hebrew data record a second spelling of "to pass." The Greek ends the clause with "to wearing out."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("to pass" legible, spelled with a waw)
readings.en: he will not again pass through you
readings.plain: will never again pass through you

readings.w: The second spelling listed in the Ketiv/Qere notes of the Hebrew data this site draws on (STEPBible, in texts/auto)
readings.en: to pass
readings.plain: will never again pass through you

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 1:15)
readings.orig: οὐ μὴ προσθήσωσιν ἔτι τοῦ διελθεῖν διὰ σοῦ εἰς παλαίωσιν
readings.en: they will not again pass through you into wearing out
readings.plain: will never again pass through you to their wearing out

why: The two Hebrew spellings are the same word, and the scroll uses the fuller one; the meaning does not change. The Greek renders beliyya'al as a phrase meaning "to wearing out" (apparently from a root meaning "wear out") and so loses the name-like "worthless one" that ties 1:15 to 1:11.

t: A scatterer, or one who blows?
p: The Hebrew has mefits, "one who scatters." The Greek has "one who blows in your face."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (mpyts fully legible)
readings.en: a scatterer has come up against your face
readings.plain: the one who scatters

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:2)
readings.orig: ἐμφυσῶν εἰς πρόσωπόν σου, ἐξαιρούμενος ἐκ θλίψεως
readings.en: blowing into your face, delivering from affliction
readings.plain: the one who blows in your face

why: Mur88 has the same word as the Masoretic Text. The Greek translator read mappiach ("one who blows"), from the root naphach, "blow," as in blowing on a fire (Ezekiel 22:20-21). It also takes the next phrase, "guard the fortress," as "rescuing from affliction," a different sense. The Hebrew fits the context of an assault better.
b: The Greek numbers this verse 2:2 because its chapter 2 begins one verse earlier.

a: The LORD will bring back the pride of Jacob
t: Bring back the pride, or turn away the arrogance?
p: The Hebrew says the LORD restores Jacob's pride. The Greek says he turned away Jacob's arrogance.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the words "the LORD" and "the pride of Jacob" are legible)
readings.orig: כִּי שָׁב יְהוָה אֶת גְּאוֹן יַעֲקֹב
readings.en: for the LORD restores the pride of Jacob
readings.plain: The LORD will bring back the pride of Jacob

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:3)
readings.orig: ἀπέστρεψεν Κύριος τὴν ὕβριν Ἰακὼβ καθὼς ὕβριν τοῦ Ἰσραήλ
readings.en: the LORD turned away the arrogance of Jacob, as the arrogance of Israel
readings.plain: The LORD has turned away the arrogance of Jacob

why: The Hebrew verb shuv can mean "return" (to restore) or "turn away" and ga'on can be good ("majesty") or bad ("arrogance"). The Greek took both in the second sense; the Hebrew context (the plunder of the vine in the same verse, and the promise of 1:12-15) fits the first. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. The Hebrew shav is a perfect ("has restored"); the Plain English Translation reads it as a prophetic perfect ("will bring back"), since the verse follows the promises of 1:12-15.

t: Dyed red, or made of men?
p: The Hebrew letters can be read "reddened" or "from men." The Greek takes the second.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (m'dm legible)
readings.en: is reddened
readings.plain: dyed red

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:4)
readings.en: the arms of their power, out of men
readings.plain: made of men

why: The same consonants (m'dm) are read in the Masoretic Text as me'uddam, "dyed red," and by the Greek as me'adam, "from men." The next line ("scarlet") fits the red theme. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

t: Cypress spears, or horsemen?
p: The Hebrew has "cypresses" (spears of cypress wood). The Greek has "horsemen."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (the word is restored in Mur88)
readings.en: and the cypresses are made to reel
readings.plain: the cypress spears are swung

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:4)
readings.en: and the horsemen will be thrown into confusion
readings.plain: the horsemen are thrown into confusion

why: "Cypresses" (berosim) as spears is a figure for the wooden shafts; the Greek seems to have read parashim, "horsemen," which fits a battle scene. The Hebrew is the harder reading and it is the older text we have.
b: The verb hor'alu is rare; it may be "made to quiver" (spears waved) or "made to reel." Some scholars emend the text.

a: but they falter on their way
t: Stumble, or flee by day?
p: The Hebrew has the nobles stumbling on their way. The Greek has them fleeing by day and growing weak.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 spells the last word bhlkwtm (a longer form of "their going")
readings.en: they stumble in their going
readings.plain: but they falter on their way

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:6)
readings.orig: καὶ φεύξονται ἡμέρας καὶ ἀσθενήσουσιν ἐν τῇ πορίᾳ αὐτῶν
readings.en: and they will flee by day and grow weak in their journey
readings.plain: but they flee by day and grow weak on their way

why: The Ketiv/Qere notes in the Hebrew data this site draws on (STEPBible, in texts/auto) record a second spelling, "journeys" (halikhot), and Mur88 writes that longer form; the meaning is the same. The Greek "flee by day" is a freer rendering that adds a detail the Hebrew does not have. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: The gates on the rivers swing open
t: Gates of the rivers, or gates of the cities?
p: The Hebrew has the gates of the rivers. The Greek has the gates of the cities.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (sh'ry hnhrwt legible)
readings.en: the gates of the rivers are opened
readings.plain: The gates on the rivers swing open

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:7)
readings.en: the gates of the cities were opened
readings.plain: The gates of the cities swing open

why: Mur88 supports the Masoretic "rivers." The Greek may have read he'arim ("the cities") for hanneharot, or tried to make sense of an unusual phrase. "Rivers" is the harder reading and fits the water images of the book (1:8; 2:8; 3:8).

t: Settled, a name (Huzzab), or a foundation?
p: The Hebrew word hutsav is a puzzle: a verb "it is set," a name "Huzzab," or, in the Greek, "foundation."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (whtsb fully legible)
readings.en: and it is fixed: she is uncovered, she is carried up
readings.plain: It is settled

readings.w: The same letters read as a name (proposed by some commentators)
readings.en: and Huzzab [is] uncovered and carried up
readings.plain: Huzzab

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:8)
readings.orig: καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασις ἀπεκαλύφθη καὶ αὕτη ἀνέβαινεν
readings.en: and the substance (the foundation) was uncovered, and she was going up
readings.plain: Her foundation is bared

why: Mur88 has exactly the Masoretic consonants. The Plain English Translation takes hutsav as the passive of natsav, "it is set, it is decreed"; it fits the sense of a decision made. As a name, "Huzzab" would be a queen, a goddess or a name for Nineveh herself; the commentators who propose it do not agree who she is. The Greek hypostasis ("what stands under, substance") reads hutsav as a noun for what was set up.

a: Nineveh has been like a pool of water ever since she began.
t: "From her days," or "her waters"?
p: The Hebrew has Nineveh like a pool since her days. The Greek has her "waters."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (Mur88 and 4Q82 are damaged here; the printout restores some letters, which cannot be cited)
readings.en: and Nineveh is like a pool of water from the days that she [was]
readings.plain: Nineveh has been like a pool of water ever since she began.

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:9)
readings.orig: καὶ Νινευή, ὡς κολυμβήθρα ὕδατος τὰ ὕδατα αὐτῆς
readings.en: and Nineveh, like a pool of water, her waters
readings.plain: Nineveh is like a pool of water, her waters.

why: The Masoretic mimey hi ("from the days of her") is the harder reading. The Greek reads mimeyha ("her waters"). 4QXIIg preserves the end of the verse ("and they are fleeing, Stop! Stop! and there is none who turns back") in readable letters that agree with the Masoretic Text, but the word at issue is restored there, so it is no evidence.

t: Heavy, burdened, or glory?
p: The Hebrew kaved can mean heavy, or glory. The Greek takes it as a verb: they are weighed down.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4Q82 (kbd mkl kly hmdh fully legible)
readings.en: heavy [with] every precious vessel
readings.plain: heavy with every costly thing

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:10)
readings.orig: βεβάρυνται ἐπὶ πάντα σκεύη τὰ ἐπιθυμητὰ αὐτῆς
readings.en: they are weighed down upon all her desirable vessels
readings.plain: they are weighed down with every costly thing

why: 4QXIIg has the same consonants (kbd) as the Masoretic Text; the Masoretes point them kaved, "heavy, abundant." Others have read kavod, "glory," or kibbed, "are weighed down" (the Greek's verb). Whatever the pointing, the picture is of treasure in heaps. The Greek also renders tekunah ("stock") as kosmos ("adornment").

t: Messengers, or works?
p: The Hebrew word can mean "messengers" or "work"; the Greek takes it as "works."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (ml'kkh legible)
readings.en: your messengers
readings.plain: your messengers

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 2:14)
readings.en: your works
readings.plain: your deeds

why: The Hebrew letters ml'kkh are read in the Masoretic Text as mal'akhekhah, "your messengers," and the Greek translator read melakhtekh, "your work." Both fit: Assyria's envoys carried its demands (2 Kings 18:17-35) and Assyria's "work" was conquest. The Greek also has "your multitude" for "her chariots" earlier in the verse, a difference that may have come from a different Hebrew word or from the Greek translator's change of the person addressed.

t: Loot, or injustice?
p: The Hebrew has peraq, a rare word for torn plunder. The Greek has "injustice."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (the word is restored in both Mur88 and 4Q82)
readings.en: full of plunder
readings.plain: full of loot

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:1)
readings.en: full of injustice
readings.plain: full of injustice

why: Pereq occurs only here and in Obadiah 14 (as "crossroads" in a different sense). The Greek rendering is a general word for the sin of which plunder is the act. Both scrolls that carry the verse have this word only as a restoration, so the older Hebrew is not shown by them.

t: Never leaves, or cannot be touched?
p: The Hebrew says the prey never departs. The Greek reads the same verb as "be felt" and says it cannot be touched.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (l' ymysh legible) and 4Q82 (lw' ymysh trp legible; the scroll spells "not" with a waw)
readings.en: the prey does not depart
readings.plain: the prey never goes away

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:1)
readings.en: prey will not be felt (touched)
readings.plain: the prey cannot be touched

why: The consonants ymysh can be pointed yamish ("depart," from mush) or yamush ("be felt," from another sense of the same root). Both scrolls agree with the Masoretic consonants. The Hebrew sense, a city that never lets its prey go, fits the verse; the Greek makes the prey untouchable.

a: There is no end to the bodies
t: No end to the corpses, or to "her nations"?
p: The Hebrew word gewiyah means "corpse." The Greek reads the same letters as "her nation" and says there is no end to her nations.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (w'yn ... lgwyh, with "no" and the final word readable)
readings.en: and there is no end to the corpse
readings.plain: There is no end to the bodies

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:3)
readings.orig: καὶ οὐκ ἦν πέρας τοῖς ἔθνεσιν αὐτῆς
readings.en: and there was no end to her nations
readings.plain: There is no end to her nations

why: The consonants gwyh read gewiyah ("body") or goyah ("her nation"). Mur88 reads the second occurrence of the word (bgwytm, "on their bodies") the same way, and the next clause confirms "corpse." The Greek then ends the verse with "they will grow weak in their bodies from the many acts of prostitution," which it takes from the first words of the next verse (see 3:4).
b: A Ketiv/Qere note in the Hebrew data this site draws on (STEPBible, in texts/auto) says that the verb "stumble" at the end of the verse is written with a conjunction in one form ("and they stumble") and with an imperfect in another ("they will stumble"); Mur88's letter for this word is restored and so cannot decide.

a: All because of the many acts of prostitution of the prostitute
t: Where does the sentence begin?
p: The Greek puts the opening words of the Hebrew verse 4 at the end of verse 3 and begins verse 4 with "A prostitute."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (mrb znwny zwnh twbt hn b'lt readable)
readings.en: from the multitude of the prostitutions of the prostitute, good of grace
readings.plain: All because of the many acts of prostitution of the prostitute

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:3-4)
readings.orig: ἀπὸ πλήθους πορνείας· πόρνη καλὴ καὶ ἐπιχαρής
readings.en: from the multitude of prostitution. A beautiful and charming prostitute
readings.plain: A prostitute

why: The Hebrew verse division puts "because of the many acts of prostitution" as the cause of what follows; it explains the woes of 3:1-3. The Greek reads it as the cause of the weakness at the end of verse 3 and starts verse 4 with the woman. The Hebrew division is followed; the Greek division shows a different understanding of how the sentence runs.

a: Are you any better than Thebes
t: Better than Thebes, or "prepare a portion"?
p: The Hebrew asks if Nineveh is better than Thebes. The Greek reads the first words as commands and makes Ammon a name.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (hatityvi legible; "from No Amon" is a restoration)
readings.en: are you better than No-amon
readings.plain: Are you any better than Thebes

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:8)
readings.orig: ἑτοίμασαι μερίδα, ἅρμοσαι χορδήν, ἑτοίμασαι μερίδα, Ἀμμών
readings.en: prepare a portion, fit a string, prepare a portion, Ammon
readings.plain: Prepare a share, tune a string, prepare a share, Ammon

why: The Greek translator did not recognize the city name No and took the letters as manah ("portion") and as a verb of preparing, keeping only "Ammon" as a name. Jeremiah 46:25 and Ezekiel 30:14-16 have the same city under the name No, so the Hebrew is easily understood.
b: The name No' 'Amon is unlike the usual Egyptian name for Thebes, Waset; it is Hebrew for "the city of Amon," after Thebes' chief god.

t: Rampart the sea, or rampart of water?
p: The Masoretic Text has "sea" twice. The printout of Mur88 has one word fewer.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: whose rampart [was] sea, from sea her wall
readings.plain: her outer defense the sea

readings.w: Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (a Hebrew scroll of the Twelve, early second century AD) (the printout shows chyl mym chwmth, without the first ym)
readings.en: a rampart of water, her wall
readings.plain: her outer defense water

why: In the Masoretic Text the first yam ("sea") has no counterpart in the Mur88 printout; the Greek ("whose beginning was the sea, and water her walls") has the sea and the water, so it sides with the Masoretic Text. The difference is small. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text and reads the second word as "water" (mayim), as the Greek does.

a: Put and the Libyans were your helpers
t: "Your" helpers, or "her" helpers?
p: The Hebrew changes to "your help" without warning. The Greek has "her helpers."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (hyw b'zrtk readable)
readings.en: Put and the Libyans were in your help
readings.plain: Put and the Libyans were your helpers

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:9)
readings.en: and the Libyans became her helpers
readings.plain: Put and the Libyans were her helpers

why: Mur88 has the second-person suffix of the Masoretic Text. The Greek uses the third person and fits the pronouns around it. The Hebrew is the harder reading, and a sudden turn from "her" to "your" is common in poetry. If it is original, the "you" is either Thebes spoken to directly, or Nineveh, who also had allies. The Greek also has "no end of flight" for "Put," reading the name as a common word.

t: Hidden, or overlooked?
p: The Hebrew says Nineveh will be hidden. The Greek says she will be overlooked, or despised.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("you also," "you will be" and "you will seek" legible; "you will be drunk," "hidden" and "stronghold" restored)
readings.en: you will be hidden
readings.plain: You will be hidden away.

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:11)
readings.en: and you will be overlooked
readings.plain: You will be overlooked.

why: The Greek verb means "look past, disregard, despise." It may be a loose rendering of "hidden" or may reflect another reading; the cause is not clear. The scroll is restored at this word and cannot decide. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The Hebrew line is "you too will be drunk; you will be hidden." The Greek is "and you will be drunk and overlooked."

t: "Are women," or "like women"?
p: The Hebrew says your people are women. The Greek says they are "like women." Mur88 writes "to your enemies" with a different preposition.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ("look," "in your midst," "the gates of" and "it will consume" legible; "your people" and "women" restored)
readings.en: your people are women
readings.plain: they are women

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:13)
readings.en: your people are like women
readings.plain: they are like women

why: The Hebrew is a flat metaphor ("are women"); the Greek adds "like" and softens it to a simile. In Mur88 the legible word before "enemies" is 'el ("to") where the Masoretic Text has l- ("to"); the sense is the same. The scroll's words for "your people" and "women" are restored, so it cannot be cited for them.
b: The whole Greek line is "look, your people are like women in you."

t: "Lie still," or "he put them to sleep"?
p: The Hebrew says the nobles settle down. The Greek says the king of Assyria put them to sleep.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 ('dyryk legible; the verb is restored)
readings.en: your nobles dwell [at rest]
readings.plain: Your great men lie still

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's printed Greek, mainly Codex Vaticanus) (Nahum 3:18)
readings.orig: βασιλεὺς Ἀσσύριος, ἐκοίμισεν τοὺς δυνάστας σου
readings.en: the king of Assyria put your rulers to sleep
readings.plain: The king of Assyria has put your great men to sleep

why: The Greek takes "king of Assyria" not as a person addressed ("Your shepherds are sleeping, king of Assyria") but as the subject of the next verb. The Hebrew keeps the address, which gives the book its last taunt to a named king. The verb "settle" (shakan) is often "dwell"; in this context it means to lie still in death.
